lessons.title: Operating and Financial Leverage: Why Cyclical Profits Swing Harder Than Revenue

body.text: Revenue is not what makes a cyclical dangerous. Fixed costs and debt are. They sit between revenue and profit like a magnifying glass, so a 10% fall in sales can wipe out half the profit.

children.text: In Chapter 1, CycleCo's revenue fell 16% in one year while its profit fell nearly 69%. That gap was not an accident of the example. It comes from two forces you can measure for any company: operating leverage, which comes from fixed operating costs, and financial leverage, which comes from interest on debt. Understand these two and you will know in advance how violently a company's earnings will react to the cycle.
Fixed Costs vs Variable Costs

markDefs.definition: Revenue minus variable costs. It is the amount left over to pay fixed costs, interest, and tax, and then become profit.

children.text: Variable costs rise and fall with sales: raw materials, freight, packaging. Fixed costs stay roughly the same whether a plant runs at 90% or 60% of capacity: salaries, plant maintenance, depreciation, lease rentals. What is left after variable costs is the
contribution
. The higher a company's fixed costs relative to its contribution, the more its profit swings when sales move.

columns.label: High fixed cost businesses
points: Cement and steel plants that must run near capacity to cover depreciation and upkeep
Airlines like InterGlobe Aviation, with aircraft leases and crew costs that do not stop when demand drops
Auto makers with large factories and dealer networks
Hotels, where the building costs the same whether rooms are full or empty

columns.label: Low fixed cost businesses
points: FMCG companies that outsource part of their manufacturing
Distributors and traders, whose main cost is the goods they resell
IT services firms, which can slow hiring and use variable pay when demand weakens

children.text: Worked Example: Same Operating Profit, Very Different Risk

CementCo and StapleCo are illustrative companies. Both have revenue of ₹10,000 crore and identical operating profit (EBIT) of ₹1,500 crore. The difference is what sits underneath. CementCo has heavy fixed costs and debt. StapleCo has mostly variable costs and no debt. Tax is 25% for both.
Now a slowdown cuts revenue by 10% for both, with variable costs falling in proportion and fixed costs and interest unchanged.

body.caption: After a 10% fall in revenue, ₹ crore (illustrative)

children.text: Same revenue shock, same starting EBIT. CementCo's net profit halves. StapleCo's falls by a sixth. The difference is entirely cost structure and debt.
Measuring the Magnifier: DOL, DFL, and DTL

markDefs.definition: Degree of Operating Leverage: the percentage change in EBIT for a 1% change in revenue, driven by fixed operating costs.
Degree of Financial Leverage: the percentage change in profit before tax for a 1% change in EBIT, driven by fixed interest costs.

children.text: Three ratios capture the magnification.
DOL
measures how fixed operating costs amplify revenue changes into EBIT changes.
DFL
measures how interest amplifies EBIT changes into PBT changes. Multiply them and you get the Degree of Total Leverage, DTL: how many percent PBT moves for every 1% move in revenue.

body.caption: All three are measured at the current level of revenue
Leverage ratios in the base year

cells: A 1% revenue change moves EBIT about 2.67%

body.title: Change in PBT for a Given Change in Revenue (Illustrative)

children.text: Leverage cuts both ways. In an upcycle, CementCo's PBT doubles on a 20% revenue rise, which is why cyclical stocks can multiply in a boom. In a downturn, a 20% revenue fall takes PBT to zero. Investors who only see the boom-year earnings growth are looking at half the picture.

body.title: Apply Total Leverage
body.prompt: An auto company has a DOL of 3 and a DFL of 2. A slowdown cuts its revenue by 8%. By approximately what percentage will its profit before tax fall? Enter the size of the fall as a positive number.
body.explanation: DTL = DOL × DFL = 3 × 2 = 6. A 1% revenue change moves PBT about 6%, so an 8% revenue fall cuts PBT by about 6 × 8 = 48%. Nearly half the pre-tax profit gone on a single-digit sales decline.

body.text: Leverage ratios are not constant. They get bigger as profits shrink. At CementCo's reduced revenue of ₹9,000 crore, DOL rises to 3,600 / 1,100 = 3.27 and DFL to 1,100 / 400 = 2.75. The closer a company gets to breakeven, the more violently each further rupee of lost revenue hits profit. That is why the second year of a downturn often hurts cyclicals more than the first.

children.text: Breakeven: How Much Revenue Can a Company Lose?

body.caption: Contribution margin ratio = Contribution ÷ Revenue. Drop interest from the top to find EBIT breakeven instead.

body.title: Why a price fall hurts more than a volume fall

children.text: The example above assumed revenue fell because volumes fell, so variable costs fell with it. Deep cyclicals often suffer the opposite: they keep selling the same tonnes, but at a lower price. Then variable costs do not fall at all, and the entire revenue loss drops straight to EBIT.

content.caption: CementCo: 10% revenue fall from price vs volume, ₹ crore

children.text: This is why steel, aluminium, and commodity chemical companies can swing into losses so quickly. When global prices fall, their input costs such as coking coal or power do not always fall at the same time or by the same amount.
Financial Leverage: The Debt Amplifier

Operating leverage is mostly built into an industry. You cannot run a steel plant without a blast furnace. Financial leverage is a management choice, and it is the one that turns a hard downturn into a crisis. Indian markets have seen this repeatedly: companies in steel, power, infrastructure, and real estate that borrowed heavily during the 2000s boom found that interest costs did not shrink when demand did. Some needed years of asset sales and restructuring; others ended up in insolvency proceedings.

body.title: Two Cement Companies, One Downturn
body.scenario: Two cement companies each report EBIT of ₹2,000 crore. Company X is nearly debt-free, with interest of ₹50 crore a year. Company Y funded a big capacity expansion with borrowings and pays ₹1,200 crore a year in interest. A construction slowdown cuts EBIT at both companies by 40%, to ₹1,200 crore.
body.prompt: Calculate what happens to each company's profit before tax. What does this tell you about how to pick between cyclicals?
body.modelAnswer: Company X: PBT falls from 2,000 - 50 = ₹1,950 crore to 1,200 - 50 = ₹1,150 crore, a fall of about 41%. Company Y: PBT falls from 2,000 - 1,200 = ₹800 crore to 1,200 - 1,200 = zero, a 100% fall. Same industry, same operating shock, but Company Y's shareholders are left with nothing, and any further dip means losses and possible pressure from lenders. When you must own a cyclical, the balance sheet is the single biggest lever you control: low-debt cyclicals survive downturns and can even buy distressed capacity cheaply, while highly leveraged ones can be forced to dilute shareholders or sell assets at the worst time.

body.title: Reducing the Swing
body.question: Which change would lower a company's Degree of Total Leverage the most without changing its revenue?
options: Raising fresh debt to buy back shares
Converting fixed-salary staff to a larger variable pay component and repaying debt
Building a new plant with higher fixed depreciation
Shifting from outsourced to in-house manufacturing
body.explanation: Variable pay reduces fixed operating costs, lowering DOL, and repaying debt reduces interest, lowering DFL. Every other option adds fixed costs or interest, which increases total leverage.

body.title: Estimate Leverage From Screener.in
steps: Open the company's Profit and Loss table on Screener.in
Pick two consecutive years and calculate the percentage change in Sales and in Operating Profit
Divide the Operating Profit change by the Sales change to estimate DOL; for example, sales up 12% and operating profit up 30% gives about 2.5
Repeat for a year when sales fell, since leverage often shows more clearly in down years
Divide Operating Profit minus Depreciation (roughly EBIT) by Profit before tax to estimate DFL
Check the Balance Sheet's Borrowings row over 5 years to see whether financial leverage is rising or falling
Compare the results with a peer in the same industry before drawing conclusions

points: Fixed operating costs create operating leverage; interest on debt creates financial leverage
DOL = Contribution ÷ EBIT, DFL = EBIT ÷ PBT, and DTL = DOL × DFL tells you how many percent PBT moves for each 1% change in revenue
Leverage magnifies both booms and busts, and it grows larger as profits approach breakeven
Price-driven revenue falls hurt far more than volume-driven falls, because variable costs do not shrink
Operating leverage is largely set by the industry; financial leverage is a management choice and the key risk you can screen for

body.text: CementCo, StapleCo, and the two cement companies are illustrative. Real companies do not disclose a clean split of fixed and variable costs, so estimates from Screener.in data are approximations. This lesson is educational and not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
